newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: FAMILY DEMANDS CRIMINAL CHARGES OVER BRIDGE COLLAPSE DEATH
The family of a Melbourne woman wants criminal charges laid over her death, after a bridge collapse at the Maccabiah Games in Israel
Elizabeth Sawicki died from swallowing polluted water, when the bridge fell into a river, at the opening ceremony of the games.
Her family has returned from Israel, landing at Melbourne airport this morning.
Mrs Sawicki's brother-in law, Mark, says the family at first believed she would recover.
He says her condition deteriorated and it was very hard to accept when she died after being put on a life support machine. - - - -
IMMIGRATION CUTS ACHIEVED
The Federal Immigration Minister, Phillip Ruddock, says the 1996/97 migration program has been delivered on target.
He says the outcome of nearly 74,000 is down by 8,600 on the previous year.
Mr Ruddock says the Government has delivered a smaller and more tightly focussed program, with more emphasis on skilled migrants.
The Minister has also announced he has accepted recommendations from a committee formed to help employers address skills shortages.
He says those include the need for speed, flexibility, and simplicity in procedures.
UNIFORM LAWS ON FOOD CONTAMINATION
Uniform national and state laws regarding the contamination of goods are proposed, following the Arnotts biscuits scare this year.
The proposal includes 10 years' jail for contaminating or threatening to contaminate goods to cause public alarm or financial loss.
A discussion paper is being released for public comment.
South Australian Attorney General, Trevor Griffin, says the Arnotts case shows there are legal problems with current laws, when there is no specific offence.
He says there could be difficulties prosecuting on charges of blackmail or extortion, where the offender's demands are not for money, but for police action.
ENGINEERS WANT COMPULSORY DUAL FRONT AIRBAGS
The Institute of Engineers wants dual front airbags made compulsory in all new cars by the turn of the century.
It says the latest round of New Car Assessment Program tests shows the combined use of airbags and seatbelts reduce the risk of severe head injury by half.
Airbags in new cars have been made compulsory in the United States, but in Australia only slightly more than 60 per cent of all new cars sold last year had them.
The Chair of the Institute's Biomechanics Panel, Dr Lynne Bilston, says there's also consumer resistance to airbags available as an optional extra.
She says people with small cars think they don't need an air bag because they're "just going to drive around town."
Dr Bilston says the extra cost for an airbag varies between about $600 and about $1,000.
"But they really do make a difference," she said.
MELBOURNE STRIKE CAUSES RUSH HOUR CONGESTION
Melbourne's traffic has returned to normal, after heavy congestion and long delays this morning, because of the 24 hour public transport strike.
Vicroads says traffic is moving freely on all the major arterials, and no further problems are expected until about three-thirty, when the afternoon rush begins.
Then, heavy traffic and delays are likely until at least seven o'clock.
Vicroads Section Leader, Geoff McKernan, says overall, there were few problems this morning.
He says the peak hour started about an hour earlier than usual, and the only real problem was an accident on the south-eastern arterial.
POLICIES ON WOMEN DEFENDED
The Head of the Office of the Status of Women, Pru Goward, says she's not concerned by United Nations criticism of the Federal Government's policies on women.
The United Nations Committee for the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women, has expressed concern over an apparent reversal in easures to achieve equality.
But Ms Goward says there are a number of good policies in place and there is no suggestion the Government is rolling back past reforms.
She's told ABC Radio the Committee's report was partly based on alarmist assessments by non-government women's organisations.
She says the UN Committee also said the Australian Government was doing a fair number of pretty good things for the status of women.
BAIL CONTINUED FOR ACCUSED IN BURNING CASE
A judge in the Townsville Supreme Court has refused to revoke the bail granted to a man accused of an attack which allegedly resulted in a girl receiving severe burns.
Conditional bail had been granted to 52-year-old Graham Akrill at an earlier court appearance, pending a psychiatric report on whether he was considered to be a threat to the comunity.
Today Jutice Cullinane ruled that there was nothing in the report which was adverse and that bail should continue, subject to the same conditions.
The report will now be sealed and not opened again unless by an order from the court.
Meanwhile 10-year-old burns victim Samantha Green remains in a stable condition and will undergo the first of a series of skin grafts tomorrow.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
